questions.q: Which four criteria does this lesson say to weigh before picking a model?
options: Capabilities, speed, cost, and effort
Color scheme, font, logo, and branding
Country of origin, release date, popularity, and price only
Number of parameters only
questions.explain: Capabilities, speed, cost, and the effort/tuning parameter are the four criteria drawn directly from Anthropic's own 'choosing a model' documentation.

questions.q: What does the lesson say is often a better first lever than switching to an entirely different model tier?
options: Switching providers immediately
Tuning an effort parameter that trades intelligence for latency/cost within the same model
Always picking the cheapest model regardless of task
Ignoring cost entirely
questions.explain: Several models expose an effort parameter that adjusts intelligence vs. latency/cost within the same model — tuning that is often a better first step than jumping to a different tier.

questions.q: In the worked example, which strategy fits a high-volume FAQ chatbot best?
options: Capability-first, starting with the flagship tier
Efficiency-first, starting with the fastest/cheapest tier
Randomly rotating between all available tiers
Using the open-weight model with the largest parameter count available
questions.explain: A high-volume, low-complexity, latency-sensitive task like an FAQ chatbot fits the efficiency-first strategy: start cheap and fast, upgrade only if testing reveals a real gap.

questions.q: In the worked example, which strategy fits a multi-step coding agent refactoring a large, unfamiliar codebase?
options: Capability-first, starting with the flagship tier
Efficiency-first, starting with the cheapest tier
No model is appropriate for this task
Only an open-weight model can do this task
questions.explain: Long-horizon reasoning, high accuracy needs, and tool use point to capability-first: start with the flagship tier, then look for room to downgrade once the workflow is proven.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what should actually decide whether to upgrade or switch models in production?
options: A provider's own marketing benchmark alone
A benchmark/evaluation set built from your own real use case, tested with your actual prompts and data
Whichever model launched most recently
Flipping a coin
questions.explain: The lesson stresses that a good evaluation set built from your own real use case — not a marketing benchmark — is the most important input for deciding whether to change models.
